opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the more important questions, and I'd frame it around how much compute we expect to be available. If you look at the trends, the compute used to train frontier models has been growing at something like four to five times per year for over a decade. If that roughly continues, and I think there are good reasons to expect it can through the end of the decade, though it gets harder with power, chip production, and capital constraints, then by 2030 we could see training runs several thousand times larger than today's largest.

What does that buy you in terms of autonomy? So far, scaling has given us models that are very good at short-horizon tasks: answering a question, writing a function, summarizing a document. Where they've struggled is long-horizon, multi-step work, where you have to plan, notice your mistakes, recover, and keep coherent over hours or days. But that's improving. The length of tasks these systems can reliably complete has been growing quite steadily, and I don't see an obvious reason it should suddenly stop.

So my expectation is that by 2030 we'll have systems that can take on tasks a skilled human would need days or maybe weeks to do, especially in software, research assistance, and other digital work, and carry them through with fairly limited oversight. That's a qualitative shift from a tool you prompt to something more like a remote worker you delegate to.

I want to be careful, though. There's real uncertainty. Some of the progress in agency will depend not just on raw scale but on things like reinforcement learning on long-horizon tasks, better scaffolding, and access to the right training environments, and those are less predictable than pre-training trends. There's also a gap between what's technically possible and what gets deployed, because of reliability, liability, and organizations adapting slowly.

But if you ask me where the default trajectory points, I'd say substantially autonomous AI agents doing economically meaningful work by 2030 is a quite plausible outcome, more plausible than many people outside the field assume. And that has big implications, both for the economy, since we could start to see automation of a meaningful share of cognitive labor, and for safety, because the more independently these systems act, the more it matters that we can actually understand and control what they're doing.

r001.rationale: The response discusses task length and says future systems may need limited oversight, but it does not characterize capacity in terms of the time between required human interventions.

r002.rationale: It says the length of tasks systems can reliably complete has been growing and predicts they could carry out work lasting days or weeks with fairly limited oversight by 2030.

r003.rationale: The response notes uncertainty about agency progress and deployment, but it does not specifically express uncertainty about roughly 10,000-fold scaling yielding drop-in remote workers; it predicts systems needing limited oversight and calls the outcome plausible.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the short answer is I expect quite a lot of change, and the way I think about it is in terms of the length and complexity of tasks that systems can handle without a human stepping in.

Right now, if you look at the frontier models, they're very capable on tasks that take a human maybe minutes to an hour or so. They can write a function, debug something fairly contained, draft a document. But when you ask them to do something that unfolds over days or weeks, where you need to maintain context, recover from mistakes, decide what to do next when the plan doesn't work, they tend to fall apart. The errors compound.

What we've been seeing, and what we've tried to measure, is that this horizon has been growing pretty steadily. The length of task that models can reliably complete has been roughly doubling on a timescale of something like half a year to a year, depending on how you measure it. And that's been driven by a combination of things: raw compute scaling, better post-training, and especially the reinforcement learning on agentic tasks that labs are now pouring resources into.

So if you just extrapolate that, by 2030 you're talking about systems that can handle tasks that take a skilled human weeks or possibly months. That's a qualitatively different thing. That's not a tool you prompt, that's something closer to a colleague you delegate to.

Now, I want to be careful about a few things. One is that these trends could bend. Compute scaling faces real constraints: power, chips, capital. We've written about this. I think continued scaling through 2030 is plausible but it's not guaranteed at the historical rate. The second thing is that benchmark performance and real-world reliability are different. A system that completes a week-long task ninety percent of the time might not be deployable if the ten percent failures are costly or hard to detect.

But I'd say my central expectation is that by 2030, a substantial fraction of cognitive work that's done today by people at computers will be doable by AI systems operating with pretty minimal oversight. Software engineering is the obvious case because it's where the training signal is cleanest, but I don't think it stays confined there. And once you have systems that can work independently for long stretches, you get this compounding effect where they can also be deployed to accelerate AI research itself, which is the thing I think people should be paying the most attention to.

r001.rationale: The response frames independent-work capacity as the length of tasks models can handle before a human needs to step in.

r002.rationale: It describes the task horizon growing and predicts that by 2030 systems could handle work lasting weeks or months with minimal oversight.

r003.rationale: The response expresses uncertainty about whether scaling will continue at its historical rate, but does not discuss roughly 10,000-fold scaling or whether it would produce drop-in remote workers by 2030.

astra-6.text:
I expect scaling to make AI systems capable of working independently for longer stretches of time. That might mean moving from tasks that take a person a few minutes to projects that take hours or days, with less human intervention along the way.

The key distinction is between being able to perform each individual step and reliably completing an entire project. If a system makes a small mistake at every stage, those mistakes can accumulate. So progress depends on systems becoming better at checking their work, recovering from errors, and recognizing when they need help, as well as becoming more capable in general.

By 2030, I think it’s plausible that we’ll see systems doing substantial pieces of software development or research with humans setting objectives and reviewing results. But I’d be cautious about treating that as a firm prediction. Scaling could contribute a lot, while the extent of independence will also depend on improvements in training and how these systems are put together.

r001.rationale: It describes independent work as lasting from minutes to hours or days, with less human intervention.

r002.rationale: It predicts that scaling will let systems work independently for longer stretches.

r003.rationale: It expresses caution about predictions for 2030, but does not address roughly 10,000-fold scaling or whether systems will function as drop-in remote workers.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the main change will be in how long these systems can work on a task without needing a human to intervene. There’s a big difference between answering a question in a few seconds and carrying out a project that takes days or weeks. The latter requires planning, keeping track of progress, recognizing mistakes, and recovering when something goes wrong.

By 2030, I’d expect scaling to make systems substantially better at those things, especially when combined with training on tasks that reward successful independent work. You could imagine giving a system a software development project, having it implement a solution, run tests, and iterate with relatively little supervision.

But I wouldn’t assume that progress will be uniform. A system might be very capable at a well-specified technical task and still struggle with an ambiguous assignment where it has to work out what someone actually wants. So my expectation is much longer stretches of useful autonomous work, with considerable uncertainty about how broadly that will translate into replacing entire jobs.

r001.rationale: It defines independent work by how long a system can work on a task without a human needing to intervene.

r002.rationale: It predicts scaling will enable substantially longer stretches of useful autonomous work with little supervision.

r003.rationale: It expresses uncertainty about whether autonomy will translate into replacing entire jobs, but does not address roughly 10,000-fold scaling or whether systems will function as drop-in remote workers by 2030.
